chapters.text: When a light moves in a game, why can brightness remain on a wall while a shadow follows the change? We will connect DOOM’s sector brightness to Quake’s lightmaps, real-time shadows, and the ordering of forward and deferred shading. You will be able to distinguish stored data from per-frame work and identify where an image’s limitations come from. Let us begin with a single surface.

A game image consists of small color cells called pixels. Filling them produces one frame, and displaying successive frames creates motion. Rendering turns the scene into an image. Start by asking what should appear at one position in this view. Making a pixel starts with identifying the visible surface. The next task is estimating how much light that surface sends toward the camera. A 3D object’s surface is divided into small triangles. Rasterization projects them onto the flat image and finds the samples they cover. A depth test helps select the surface in front when surfaces overlap. Follow the surfaces visible to the camera. Objects are three-dimensional, but the image is flat, so front and back surfaces can overlap at one image location. Depth distinguishes their order. A normal instead describes surface orientation. Position, depth and direction are different inputs to shading. Visibility alone does not calculate lighting. Position, surface normal, material, and light data are needed to determine color. The normal describes a surface’s orientation. Imagine illuminating paper head-on, then at a slant. A dot product measures how closely the directions align. For two arrows normalized to length one, alignment gives one and a sixty-degree angle gives 0.5. In this simple model, with other inputs fixed, the directional contribution is halved. A vector is an arrow with a direction and length. A unit vector has length one, allowing us to compare direction without mixing in length. Good alignment does not guarantee illumination: a wall in between can block the light. Directional response and visibility are separate tests. The long equation is a ledger of light. It adds emitted light to light arriving from elsewhere and reflected toward us. The material determines how much is reflected. The integral indicates that contributions from many directions are combined. You do not need to memorize the equation. Follow three questions: which surface is visible, can light reach it, and how does that surface reflect it? Games may recompute these answers or store some of them in advance. Switching to a reflection diagnostic changes how the same surfaces appear. Distinguish the final game view from a diagnostic view. A ray is a test line extending from a point in a direction. From the camera it can find the first visible object; from a surface toward a light it can test for blockers. A reflected ray can find an object visible in a mirror. A rasterized image can still use ray-based calculations. Rays may compute lighting before gameplay, while the running game reads the stored result. Our first choice replaces complex light transport with a brightness value assigned to each part of the world.

DOOM’s basic 1993 lighting starts with a sector brightness value. The map assigns brightness to a sector, and the renderer uses it to choose a color table. A colormap provides colors that display the same wall pattern at different brightnesses. The code’s bit shift groups sector brightness into coarse levels to form an index. Extra lighting and orientation adjustments are applied, with the index restricted to its valid range. Horizontal and vertical walls receive different adjustments. This is an axis-based rule, rather than a continuous calculation of the angle to a light. Two perpendicular walls can appear at different brightness in the same sector. The sector has not changed; the wall orientation changes the color-table selection. This is a simple orientation distinction rather than continuous lighting over a curved surface. Distance-related behavior also enters through scale-dependent color-table selection. Reducing the process to a single sector lookup would omit that stage. This is not a per-light visibility test between an object and a lamp. The scheme alone does not automatically produce a local light footprint or a precise object shadow. The footage shows the 2024 rerelease. Modern source-port lighting must be distinguished from the rules in the original 1993 code. Beyond sector brightness and wall-direction adjustments, storing small patches of light requires finer surface information.

The game Quake stores that information at locations on the wall. A texture is a digital image supplying a pattern such as bricks; a lightmap is a separate image recording illumination across the surface. Separate the pattern image from the lighting image used on the same wall. As the viewpoint moves, the pattern stays attached to the surface. Keep its texture coordinates distinct from the coordinates used to store lighting. Instead of computing every point on a continuous wall, we choose representative samples. At each sample we test visibility to the light and account for direction, distance and intensity. Computing these results before gameplay is called baking. Our diagram fills samples in sequence and transfers the results to a texture. Samples behind the box are darker because the light is blocked. Separate the repeating wall pattern from the broad illumination in these rooms. Changing the pattern does not automatically recompute lighting. Increasing lightmap resolution does not add detail to the original brick picture either. The two data sources serve different purposes. In this example, the seams between wall pieces stand out. Check whether stored lighting joins smoothly across neighboring surfaces. The visible seam alone does not establish a single cause. A wall texture may contain fine detail while its lightmap uses coarse samples. Raising texture resolution alone does not refine the lighting boundary. Raising lightmap resolution improves stored lighting detail without inventing detail in the wall texture. A later engine demonstration makes the distinction observable. The 2017 Unreal comparison rooms are labeled with lightmap resolutions of 128, 256, 512, and 1,024. Separate texture detail from lighting boundaries. The camera visits different authored rooms; this is not a single-object on/off experiment. The numbers in each room identify the displayed comparison conditions. First inspect the wall pattern, then the boundary where a shadow crosses it. The two kinds of detail need not be stored at the same density. At runtime, the renderer reads the wall pattern and the lighting value for the corresponding surface location, then combines them. Texture coordinates specify where to look in an image. The two images can use different layouts and resolutions. Inspect texture sharpness separately from lighting-edge sharpness. Direct light travels from a light to a surface. Indirect light arrives after reflecting off another surface. Quake II’s tools also computed reflected contributions between surface patches and added them to lightmap samples, illuminating places without direct exposure. Even a dark passage need not have a uniform color. Its appearance alone does not identify the algorithm used to compute indirect lighting. This should not be labeled photon mapping. Algorithms can share the goal of storing indirect light while calculating it through different processes. A similar visual impression and an identical calculation method are different claims. Thinking in separate layers explains update cost. Changing a wall texture and moving a light are different edits. The latter changes which samples receive illumination, so stored visibility and indirect lighting must be checked against the new scene. Changing a wall’s color changes a material input; moving a light changes light paths. This view lets us inspect the room’s structure and illumination. Which information needs rebuilding depends on which input was changed. Moving a light exposes the limitation: stored values describe the old configuration. New visibility and orientation require recalculation or an additional dynamic-lighting method. This is object manipulation in the editor, not a completed light-off and rebake comparison. A moving character is not attached to one wall location. Quake includes a downward query that samples surface lighting. Static surface storage and a moving object’s lighting query are separate concerns. Moving the camera does not move the stored lighting samples off the wall. We will compare how moving objects read spatial lighting later. First, consider how to read the same wall image stably when it is farther away.

The difference begins with screen cells and texture cells. A screen cell is a pixel; an image cell in a texture is a texel. A distant floor puts many texels inside one pixel. Selecting just one can change the choice with a small viewpoint movement, making the pattern shimmer. Viewed obliquely, distant road details crowd into a narrow part of the image. Selecting one texel as if it were a nearby surface cannot adequately represent that larger region. Mipmaps store progressively smaller versions of a texture. Selecting an appropriate level avoids repeatedly resolving details finer than the pixel’s footprint. Smaller mip levels combine fine details. The purpose is to choose values representing the sampled region, not to select a blurry image arbitrarily. When a value is needed between texture samples, bilinear filtering combines four neighbors. Their weights determine how much each contributes, with closer samples contributing more. This operation works within one texture level. Take a horizontal fraction of one quarter and a vertical fraction of one half. The top-left and bottom-left weights are each three eighths; the right-hand weights are each one eighth. They sum to one, and the nearer left values contribute more. A texture can hold data other than photographic color. This view separates masks packed into different channels. Red, green and blue do not automatically identify a normal map. Before interpreting filtering, identify what the blended values actually mean. As distance increases, a smaller mip level may be appropriate, but abrupt switches can be visible. Trilinear filtering blends the bilinear results from two neighboring mip levels: interpolation within each level and between levels. At an oblique viewing angle, a pixel’s footprint becomes elongated. Anisotropic filtering accounts for this directional shape instead of using only a roughly square footprint. Look at the thin stair edges at an angle. One pixel can contain both an edge and empty space. Testing one location may miss that edge; testing coverage at several locations can represent it more consistently. This motivates multisampling later. Texture filtering instead combines values from a surface texture. Filtering reads stored information stably rather than inventing missing detail. Higher quality may require reading and blending more samples. Where data is gathered and the order of processing therefore also matter. Tile-based rendering organizes that work by regions of the screen.

It divides the image into small tiles and bins the triangles covering each tile. Alongside how lighting is calculated, we are considering how the required data is processed. Tilting the camera toward the building changes the geometry covering the image. Classifying those triangles by the image region they affect is the starting point for our tile explanation. This engine view is not an execution trace of historical PowerVR hardware. The 1990s PowerVR lineage illustrates this hardware approach. We will not project the complete structure of a modern programmable renderer onto those earlier devices. Repeatedly moving data to and from external memory costs bandwidth. Keeping a small tile’s working data in nearby on-chip storage can reduce those trips. The tile is completed and its result is then written out. Shading computes a surface’s color and illumination. PowerVR’s TBDR resolves visibility before performing needed shading. Deferred means postponed. The later technique called deferred shading postpones a different part of the work. The list here contains primitives. Tiled lighting instead lists lights affecting a screen region. Similar-looking grids can contain different data for different purposes. Color calculation can be skipped for opaque surfaces hidden behind a wall, while transparent or discarded fragments need different handling. Other GPUs also use early depth tests and caches, so tiling alone does not determine performance. So far, we have selected surfaces visible to the camera.

Whether a light reaches that visible surface is a different question. DOOM 3 in 2004 updates direct lighting and shadows as lights and objects move. Distinguish that task from reading previously stored indirect lighting. Inspect the lit surfaces from the moving viewpoint. A simple diffuse model receives more direct light when its normal faces the light. That example does not describe every material or effect in the game. A normal map stores small-scale surface orientation in a texture. It can produce rock-like shading without automatically changing a flat surface’s outer silhouette. Official DOOM 3 game footage moves through dark industrial spaces and shows illuminated characters and structures. We first observe that appearance, then examine shadow construction through released source and our diagram. Game pixels alone do not reveal every stencil operation. While moving, distinguish surface brightness from the object’s silhouette. The next diagram constructs the space behind that boundary. Put a hand in front of a flashlight and a region behind it loses that light. Shadow volumes construct this region in 3D. Edges on the light-facing silhouette are extruded and connected into side faces, as seen in DOOM 3’s public code. We test whether the visible surface point lies inside that region. The stencil buffer stores test values at image locations. If a point is in shadow, that light’s contribution is omitted; this is not simply a black image pasted onto the scene. The stencil test is not simply painting the volume sides black. It counts how the test path crosses front and back faces to determine whether a sample is inside the shadowed region. Camera-inside cases also require careful counting direction and cap handling. A point-light assumption produces sharp boundaries, and large screen coverage can increase cost. Real-time direct lighting does not by itself solve indirect reflections or color bleeding. Separate the robot’s interior shading from its silhouette. Changing the directions used for lighting can suggest grooves, but it does not create the actual protruding shape visible in silhouette. Normal mapping changes shading directions, not the underlying geometry.

Half-Life 2 illustrates another 2004 choice: richer use of baked lighting. Responding to normal-map orientation requires more information than one brightness value. Notice the impression that the character and background occupy one space. That does not mean static walls and moving characters must retrieve lighting from the same storage. We will separate directional components from spatial samples. A single brightness value cannot describe how brightness changes with surface orientation. Slowly tilt a sheet under a flashlight. Facing the beam concentrates it into a smaller area, while a tilt spreads the same beam across a larger area. The amount received by a small part of the sheet therefore changes. An arrow perpendicular to the sheet is a normal. Here we use a unit normal with length one. Draw another unit arrow from the surface toward the light. Parallel arrows mean the sheet faces the light directly, and a wider angle means more oblique illumination. The incoming ray travels opposite to the direction from the surface toward the light. The dot product measures how aligned two directions are. For two unit arrows it equals the cosine of their angle. Zero degrees gives one, sixty gives one half, and ninety gives zero. Under otherwise equal conditions this is the directional factor for diffuse direct light. Light intensity and material must also be included to obtain the final displayed brightness. Precomputed lighting needs more than one brightness value to retain directional response. Half-Life 2 radiosity normal mapping stores lighting colors for three reference directions in a surface-attached coordinate system. These directions form a basis. The three arrows are not new lamps; they are reference directions for reading stored lighting as the surface direction changes. Now enlarge one point on the wall. It has three stored lighting components. Compare its normal-map direction with basis 1, then compute dot products with basis 2 and 3. Clamp negative values to zero. These weights determine each stored value’s contribution and need not sum to 1 like probabilities. Let us calculate just the red color channel. Set the stored values to 0.8, 0.2 and 0.1. With the normal equal to basis 1, weights are 1, 0 and 0, giving 0.8. Rotate 30° toward basis 2: the weights become about 0.866, 0.5 and 0. Only the normal changed; the stored values stayed fixed. Multiply each stored value by its weight and add the contributions. 0.8 × 0.866 + 0.2 × 0.5 is approximately 0.793. The formula abbreviates these three multiplications and additions. For real colors, repeat the operation for red, green and blue. These are illustrative values, not measured game brightness. Use the same coordinate frame, clamp each dot product to 0–1, then multiply and sum the stored colors. This is the method in Valve’s published 2004 code. Substituting squared weights from another formulation changes the result. We can now follow why small bumps change shading while the stored colors remain unchanged. The final image does not display directional lighting components separately. The game shows the result; the diagram separates the intermediate values producing it. Reading them together makes the storage scheme meaningful. A weight is a mixing proportion. Even with the same ingredients, changing their proportions changes the result. Directional lightmaps give more weight to components aligned with the surface. Here the robot is inspected from different viewpoints. Distinguish surface orientation from camera motion. Materials and lighting also affect the real image. Our diagram isolates surface direction so stored values and the weights used to read them can be considered separately. Changing the normal changes the directional contributions. This adds small-scale orientation response beyond one flat brightness value, without reconstructing geometry or every dynamic occlusion. A single combined value loses directional information. Keeping separate directional components allows a surface to select more of the contribution it faces. This does not independently generate new moving shadows. The game shows completed shading; the diagram separates the directional contributions. Our spatial diagram separates a rock-like surface into actual geometry and normal-map detail. Changing normal arrows affects internal shading while the outer silhouette remains flat. Moving real vertices also changes silhouette and occlusion. The distinction is the information each representation creates. Here we inspect the robot’s arm and torso from different directions. The outline gives clues about geometry, while small variations inside a face give clues about material and orientation. Treating them as the same thing overstates what normal maps can do. Our earlier diagram changed directions without moving the plane’s vertices. Apply the same habit of separating outline from interior detail here. A wall lightmap stays attached to the wall, but a character moves. Lighting can instead be prepared at locations in the room and nearby information retrieved. Such spatial samples are commonly called probes. The historical ambient cube and other engines’ probe systems use different representations. Think of these points as locations storing lighting information, not little light sources. A wall texture stays on a surface; these samples occupy volume, including height. A moving character uses nearby information. Interpolation combines values between samples to avoid abrupt changes. This Unreal example is a different engine from Half-Life 2. As the camera turns into the room, walls and spatial points appear together. Distinguish the lighting image attached to a wall from lighting information sampled in space. The points are not light-emitting bulbs. A later Unreal lighting demonstration displays spatial samples and moves a character between a dark room and a bright floor. A surface-texel grid and samples distributed through space store information in different locations. This is a 2017 engine example of spatial lighting, not the identical implementation of Half-Life 2 ambient cubes. First inspect the character together with the surrounding sample visualization. Locate the prepared values, then follow the character as it changes position. It cannot carry a single wall texel around the room; it needs lighting information appropriate to its location. The room interior and the floor outside have different surroundings and incoming illumination. As the character moves between them, inspect its body brightness together with its position. The displayed samples are spatial clues for this lookup, not necessarily actual light sources. Later, a changed viewpoint reveals the samples and object from another direction. Two points close in the image may be separated in depth. Unlike a surface lightmap, this distribution must be read in height as well. These operations do not measure exact interpolation weights or per-frame cost. Internal values require separate engine evidence. Finally inspect the room from another viewpoint. Consider sample placement together with the places a character can occupy. The existence of samples does not make lighting exact everywhere. Their density, placement and interpolation are further design choices. The key here is that storage is in space rather than on the wall. Higher-quality baking consumes preparation time and storage. Lower runtime cost trades against production work and update cost. One map’s bake time cannot serve as a universal figure for games. Precomputation lets the game read prepared answers. Changing the room or lighting may invalidate them. This editor view inspects a scene; its playback time is not a measurement of baking time. Light remaining after a source is disabled can also reflect different update times. Static indirect light may be stored while direct lighting is updated dynamically. Next, record depth to determine where that changing direct light is blocked. Imagine placing a camera at the light.

A shadow map records the first surface depth in each direction instead of color. Comparing a visible surface point against that depth reveals whether another object blocks the light before it arrives. In this example, smaller depth means nearer and larger means farther. A test point behind the stored surface is blocked. Just as rulers need matching origins and units, both depths must be compared using the same light-view convention. Disabling a light differs from disabling shadows. Removing the whole light contribution first darkens the terrain. After restoring it, shadow settings are changed. Distinguish shading caused by surface orientation from shadows cast when another surface blocks light. For a numerical example, stored depth of 0.33 and receiver depth of 0.80 place the receiver behind the first surface. If moving the blocker changes stored depth to 0.90, the receiver at 0.80 lies in front and is unoccluded by this test. Magnifying the light’s depth image reveals its texel grid. Covering a large region with few texels can create stair-stepped shadow edges, even when the original shape is smooth. Stored numbers have limited precision. Two computations of the same surface depth can differ slightly, making it appear to block itself. Bias adds a small adjustment to the comparison to reduce this self-shadowing error. Excessive bias can detach the shadow from the object. A single chosen value is not guaranteed to solve every distance and surface slope. A single shadow-map lookup can give a hard jagged boundary. PCF tests several nearby locations and averages the lit results. It combines comparison outcomes, rather than averaging depths before one comparison. If two of four neighboring tests report visibility, their PCF average is one half. This produces an intermediate visibility value, but does not exactly integrate every path from an area light. Wider filters require more samples and introduce further tradeoffs. A filter’s extent controls the neighborhood combined. PCSS adjusts it using the relationship between blockers and receivers. Variance shadow maps store depth’s first and second moments to approximate visibility. These are different approximations, with limitations such as light leaking in the latter. Variance Shadow Maps and Unreal’s Virtual Shadow Maps share an abbreviation but are different methods. A later episode will distinguish virtual-page shadow management.

One map covering a broad outdoor scene can make nearby shadows coarse. Cascaded Shadow Maps split the camera’s view by distance and assign shadow maps to those regions. This does not create more lights. It records shadows from one directional light at different spatial densities near and far from the camera. For an illustrative example, 2,048 texels covering 20 meters gives roughly one centimeter per texel. Covering 200 meters with the same count gives roughly ten centimeters. Those numbers are not settings or performance measurements from a game. They illustrate how coverage changes world-space texel size at the same resolution. Choose the shadow map for the point’s camera-distance interval and blend results near transitions. Tiny camera motions can make the projected grid slide and shadows shimmer, so stabilization can snap the projection to the texel grid. In the acquired official Unreal example, the character casts a visible shadow while running on the floor, but not on the stairs. The documentation describes disabled CSM reception on the stairs. That clip demonstrates receiver configuration, rather than visualizing cascade partitions. A separate spatial diagram explains the splits, while the observed engine result illustrates the setting. A 2017 official Unreal demonstration shows the partitions more directly. Enabling Show, Advanced, Shadow Frustums displays differently colored projected boundaries over the scene. Observe how those boundaries change with the shadow distance and distribution controls. The colored boundaries visualize shadow-recording regions, not additional lights. Pulling the camera back reveals the spatial separation between the nearby objects and distant terrain. The same demonstration changes the cascade count through four, zero, one, and three while also adjusting shadow distance. Distinguish disabling cascades from assigning a broad region to one map. Relate the one-versus-multiple edge comparison to our equal-resolution coverage diagram. Several controls change, so we do not attribute every difference to one parameter. Inspect near and far regions together. The total distance and distribution change as well as the number of splits. Connect each visible setting change with the affected region instead of drawing a conclusion from one still image. After the nearby region, inspect distant terrain too. These settings control distant shadow coverage and cascade count. Read the settings together with the region of the view they cover. More cascades require more maps. Managing transitions and stability allocates a budget to shadows. With multiple lights, adding their lighting contributions also has a cost.

That cost is also connected to the order of material and lighting evaluation. Forward rendering evaluates the material and relevant lights while drawing a surface. Once it handles a wall pixel, it completes the lighting calculation there to produce its color. Deferred shading postpones lighting. It first records visible-surface properties such as base color, orientation and depth by image position. This collection is the G-buffer. A later lighting stage reads those records to compute illumination. A buffer stores values for later processing. The G-buffer gathers properties of the visible surface at each image location. Colors in this material view represent specific data rather than decoration; their meaning must be identified. Connect surface information to lighting evaluation and then to the final color. Unwrapping the book assigns image locations to its 3D faces: UV coordinates. Base color describes material color, roughness the spread of reflection, and normals the orientation used in lighting. One surface can have several property images. This is an object-material demonstration, distinct from a screen-space G-buffer. Base color is not the final lit color. Normals encode orientation; roughness controls the spread of a material’s reflection. The Unreal book example inspects and exports material data separately. Object textures and the current frame’s G-buffer use different domains, but the demonstration helps distinguish property types. Follow one pixel on the same wall. Suppose two lighting contributions, already accounting for the material, are 0.25 and 0.35; their sum is 0.6. Forward computes this during surface shading. Deferred records surface data first, then combines lighting in a later stage. The goal is the same; the ordering and intermediate data differ. If a light only reaches the right wall, pixels on the left need not evaluate it. Both approaches can cull irrelevant lights. The four objects and three lights illustrate ordering, not a claim that Forward always evaluates every light or Deferred always wins. S.T.A.L.K.E.R.’s development materials describe a deferred approach for many lights. Its counts and performance figures belong to the documented scene and hardware context. A record is useful to a later operation, but writing and reading it costs work and bandwidth. The G-buffer has that tradeoff. A record of only one frontmost surface cannot by itself describe all the layers needed for transparent glass. Place two glass layers in front of an opaque wall. A buffer storing only the nearest surface does not contain every layer’s material. Compositing them needs additional information or passes. A real engine can therefore combine rendering paths within one frame. A pass is a stage or round of rendering work. An engine can shade opaque objects with Deferred and composite glass in a separate Forward pass. Light pre-pass is another compromise: lighting from depth and normals, followed by material combination. Forward remains in use. Robo Recall is a VR game whose view follows head movement. Its Forward path was chosen with multisampling and required features in mind. We use this demonstration to connect that engineering choice to visible image quality. This is actual VR interaction with objects. Inspect both the response and the image edges. This game illustrates VR’s moving thin edges. Follow the outlines of hands, robots and fragments. Image quality depends on pixel coverage as well as the order of lighting calculations. Next, inspect those edges in the magnified comparison. Anti-aliasing reduces jagged or unstable image edges. Multisampling tests coverage at several positions inside a pixel. If two of four positions are covered, the edge can contribute roughly half the coverage; this is an illustrative example, not a claim about the game’s sample setting. Observe the magnified line. Multiple coverage tests do not necessarily repeat every material and lighting computation that many times. Cost depends on implementation and settings. Forward versus Deferred is therefore a choice involving image quality, features and memory costs, not simply which name is newer. Missing screen-space features in a particular Unreal forward implementation are implementation constraints, not proof that such effects are mathematically impossible in every forward renderer. Changing diagnostic modes reveals information otherwise combined in the final image. This reflection view is not automatically screen-space reflection. Even when effect names resemble one another, their inputs and implementation must be identified. TBDR separates visibility determination from shading; deferred shading separates surface-data storage from lighting. Screen depth retained during rendering can also support effects after lighting. Use that depth to inspect a wall crevice.

Corners can still look ungrounded after direct-light shadows are drawn because they receive light from fewer surrounding directions than open areas. Screen-space ambient occlusion, or SSAO, estimates this local occlusion from screen depth. Screen-space means operating on information available in the current camera image. SSAO does not trace all lighting through the scene. It examines nearby screen-depth samples to estimate occlusion around a surface. Our diagram places samples around a box corner and compares depths. A small radius emphasizes contact; a larger one reaches farther but can increase undersampling and incorrect associations. Filtering can reduce noise but may blur across boundaries. Sample count, filtering, and depth differences must be considered together. The depth buffer primarily describes visible front surfaces. A thin rod in front of a distant wall does not reveal its thickness through a single depth value. An excessive sample range can associate unrelated surfaces and produce a dark halo around the object. CryEngine 2’s 2007 technical discussion and Unreal documentation describe screen-based approximations and their limitations. Actual comparisons need identified versions and settings. A 2017 Unreal 4.16 demonstration approaches a cube model and changes the AO Power and Bias controls. Watch the gaps between cubes and their floor contacts. Adjusting this contact treatment is different from adding a light source. Several controls and the camera change in this sequence, so we will not attribute every difference to one isolated number. First observe the actual manipulations and contacts; our separate diagram isolates sample range and the limits of depth information. This is not a substitute for direct-light shadows. Darkening corners does not calculate occlusion for a particular lamp or colored indirect light reflected from another wall. Information outside the screen and behind visible surfaces is still missing. The same information boundary becomes important for screen-space reflections in the next episode.

This episode followed assigned brightness, stored surface lighting, and updated visibility for moving lights. More lights also changed the ordering of material and lighting work. To distinguish methods, ask three questions: what is stored, which changes require recomputation, and which information is missing from the input? The next episode extends the discussion to indirect light, reflections, water, and fog, connecting photon mapping, SSR, Forward+, and clustered lighting to the different problems they address. Reading techniques through their inputs and processing order makes an engine frame easier to understand than names alone. The programming-coaching link in the description is available for hands-on learning.

The footage shows the 2024 rerelease. Modern source-port lighting must be distinguished from the rules in the original 1993 code. Beyond sector brightness and wall-direction adjustments, storing small patches of light requires finer surface information.

scenes.title: 1996–1997: 계산을 게임 앞으로 옮긴 라이트맵
lines: The game Quake stores that information at locations on the wall. A texture is a digital image supplying a pattern such as bricks; a lightmap is a separate image recording illumination across the surface. Separate the pattern image from the lighting image used on the same wall. As the viewpoint moves, the pattern stays attached to the surface. Keep its texture coordinates distinct from the coordinates used to store lighting. Instead of computing every point on a continuous wall, we choose representative samples. At each sample we test visibility to the light and account for direction, distance and intensity. Computing these results before gameplay is called baking. Our diagram fills samples in sequence and transfers the results to a texture. Samples behind the box are darker because the light is blocked. Separate the repeating wall pattern from the broad illumination in these rooms. Changing the pattern does not automatically recompute lighting. Increasing lightmap resolution does not add detail to the original brick picture either. The two data sources serve different purposes. In this example, the seams between wall pieces stand out. Check whether stored lighting joins smoothly across neighboring surfaces. The visible seam alone does not establish a single cause. A wall texture may contain fine detail while its lightmap uses coarse samples. Raising texture resolution alone does not refine the lighting boundary. Raising lightmap resolution improves stored lighting detail without inventing detail in the wall texture. A later engine demonstration makes the distinction observable. The 2017 Unreal comparison rooms are labeled with lightmap resolutions of 128, 256, 512, and 1,024. Separate texture detail from lighting boundaries. The camera visits different authored rooms; this is not a single-object on/off experiment. The numbers in each room identify the displayed comparison conditions. First inspect the wall pattern, then the boundary where a shadow crosses it. The two kinds of detail need not be stored at the same density. At runtime, the renderer reads the wall pattern and the lighting value for the corresponding surface location, then combines them. Texture coordinates specify where to look in an image. The two images can use different layouts and resolutions. Inspect texture sharpness separately from lighting-edge sharpness. Direct light travels from a light to a surface. Indirect light arrives after reflecting off another surface. Quake II’s tools also computed reflected contributions between surface patches and added them to lightmap samples, illuminating places without direct exposure. Even a dark passage need not have a uniform color. Its appearance alone does not identify the algorithm used to compute indirect lighting. This should not be labeled photon mapping. Algorithms can share the goal of storing indirect light while calculating it through different processes. A similar visual impression and an identical calculation method are different claims. Thinking in separate layers explains update cost. Changing a wall texture and moving a light are different edits. The latter changes which samples receive illumination, so stored visibility and indirect lighting must be checked against the new scene. Changing a wall’s color changes a material input; moving a light changes light paths. This view lets us inspect the room’s structure and illumination. Which information needs rebuilding depends on which input was changed. Moving a light exposes the limitation: stored values describe the old configuration. New visibility and orientation require recalculation or an additional dynamic-lighting method. This is object manipulation in the editor, not a completed light-off and rebake comparison. A moving character is not attached to one wall location. Quake includes a downward query that samples surface lighting. Static surface storage and a moving object’s lighting query are separate concerns. Moving the camera does not move the stored lighting samples off the wall. We will compare how moving objects read spatial lighting later. First, consider how to read the same wall image stably when it is farther away.

scenes.title: 라이트맵도 텍스처: 작은 픽셀이 넓은 면을 덮을 때
lines: The difference begins with screen cells and texture cells. A screen cell is a pixel; an image cell in a texture is a texel. A distant floor puts many texels inside one pixel. Selecting just one can change the choice with a small viewpoint movement, making the pattern shimmer. Viewed obliquely, distant road details crowd into a narrow part of the image. Selecting one texel as if it were a nearby surface cannot adequately represent that larger region. Mipmaps store progressively smaller versions of a texture. Selecting an appropriate level avoids repeatedly resolving details finer than the pixel’s footprint. Smaller mip levels combine fine details. The purpose is to choose values representing the sampled region, not to select a blurry image arbitrarily. When a value is needed between texture samples, bilinear filtering combines four neighbors. Their weights determine how much each contributes, with closer samples contributing more. This operation works within one texture level. Take a horizontal fraction of one quarter and a vertical fraction of one half. The top-left and bottom-left weights are each three eighths; the right-hand weights are each one eighth. They sum to one, and the nearer left values contribute more. A texture can hold data other than photographic color. This view separates masks packed into different channels. Red, green and blue do not automatically identify a normal map. Before interpreting filtering, identify what the blended values actually mean. As distance increases, a smaller mip level may be appropriate, but abrupt switches can be visible. Trilinear filtering blends the bilinear results from two neighboring mip levels: interpolation within each level and between levels. At an oblique viewing angle, a pixel’s footprint becomes elongated. Anisotropic filtering accounts for this directional shape instead of using only a roughly square footprint. Look at the thin stair edges at an angle. One pixel can contain both an edge and empty space. Testing one location may miss that edge; testing coverage at several locations can represent it more consistently. This motivates multisampling later. Texture filtering instead combines values from a surface texture. Filtering reads stored information stably rather than inventing missing detail. Higher quality may require reading and blending more samples. Where data is gathered and the order of processing therefore also matter. Tile-based rendering organizes that work by regions of the screen.

scenes.title: 1990년대의 다른 갈래: 타일 베이스드 GPU
lines: It divides the image into small tiles and bins the triangles covering each tile. Alongside how lighting is calculated, we are considering how the required data is processed. Tilting the camera toward the building changes the geometry covering the image. Classifying those triangles by the image region they affect is the starting point for our tile explanation. This engine view is not an execution trace of historical PowerVR hardware. The 1990s PowerVR lineage illustrates this hardware approach. We will not project the complete structure of a modern programmable renderer onto those earlier devices. Repeatedly moving data to and from external memory costs bandwidth. Keeping a small tile’s working data in nearby on-chip storage can reduce those trips. The tile is completed and its result is then written out. Shading computes a surface’s color and illumination. PowerVR’s TBDR resolves visibility before performing needed shading. Deferred means postponed. The later technique called deferred shading postpones a different part of the work. The list here contains primitives. Tiled lighting instead lists lights affecting a screen region. Similar-looking grids can contain different data for different purposes. Color calculation can be skipped for opaque surfaces hidden behind a wall, while transparent or discarded fragments need different handling. Other GPUs also use early depth tests and caches, so tiling alone does not determine performance. So far, we have selected surfaces visible to the camera.

scenes.title: 2004: 둠 쓰리의 법선 반응과 섀도 볼륨
lines: Whether a light reaches that visible surface is a different question. DOOM 3 in 2004 updates direct lighting and shadows as lights and objects move. Distinguish that task from reading previously stored indirect lighting. Inspect the lit surfaces from the moving viewpoint. A simple diffuse model receives more direct light when its normal faces the light. That example does not describe every material or effect in the game. A normal map stores small-scale surface orientation in a texture. It can produce rock-like shading without automatically changing a flat surface’s outer silhouette. Official DOOM 3 game footage moves through dark industrial spaces and shows illuminated characters and structures. We first observe that appearance, then examine shadow construction through released source and our diagram. Game pixels alone do not reveal every stencil operation. While moving, distinguish surface brightness from the object’s silhouette. The next diagram constructs the space behind that boundary. Put a hand in front of a flashlight and a region behind it loses that light. Shadow volumes construct this region in 3D. Edges on the light-facing silhouette are extruded and connected into side faces, as seen in DOOM 3’s public code. We test whether the visible surface point lies inside that region. The stencil buffer stores test values at image locations. If a point is in shadow, that light’s contribution is omitted; this is not simply a black image pasted onto the scene. The stencil test is not simply painting the volume sides black. It counts how the test path crosses front and back faces to determine whether a sample is inside the shadowed region. Camera-inside cases also require careful counting direction and cap handling. A point-light assumption produces sharp boundaries, and large screen coverage can increase cost. Real-time direct lighting does not by itself solve indirect reflections or color bleeding. Separate the robot’s interior shading from its silhouette. Changing the directions used for lighting can suggest grooves, but it does not create the actual protruding shape visible in silhouette. Normal mapping changes shading directions, not the underlying geometry.

scenes.title: 2004: 하프라이프 투의 방향별 베이크와 이동 물체
lines: Half-Life 2 illustrates another 2004 choice: richer use of baked lighting. Responding to normal-map orientation requires more information than one brightness value. Notice the impression that the character and background occupy one space. That does not mean static walls and moving characters must retrieve lighting from the same storage. We will separate directional components from spatial samples. A single brightness value cannot describe how brightness changes with surface orientation. Slowly tilt a sheet under a flashlight. Facing the beam concentrates it into a smaller area, while a tilt spreads the same beam across a larger area. The amount received by a small part of the sheet therefore changes. An arrow perpendicular to the sheet is a normal. Here we use a unit normal with length one. Draw another unit arrow from the surface toward the light. Parallel arrows mean the sheet faces the light directly, and a wider angle means more oblique illumination. The incoming ray travels opposite to the direction from the surface toward the light. The dot product measures how aligned two directions are. For two unit arrows it equals the cosine of their angle. Zero degrees gives one, sixty gives one half, and ninety gives zero. Under otherwise equal conditions this is the directional factor for diffuse direct light. Light intensity and material must also be included to obtain the final displayed brightness. Precomputed lighting needs more than one brightness value to retain directional response. Half-Life 2 radiosity normal mapping stores lighting colors for three reference directions in a surface-attached coordinate system. These directions form a basis. The three arrows are not new lamps; they are reference directions for reading stored lighting as the surface direction changes. Now enlarge one point on the wall. It has three stored lighting components. Compare its normal-map direction with basis 1, then compute dot products with basis 2 and 3. Clamp negative values to zero. These weights determine each stored value’s contribution and need not sum to 1 like probabilities. Let us calculate just the red color channel. Set the stored values to 0.8, 0.2 and 0.1. With the normal equal to basis 1, weights are 1, 0 and 0, giving 0.8. Rotate 30° toward basis 2: the weights become about 0.866, 0.5 and 0. Only the normal changed; the stored values stayed fixed. Multiply each stored value by its weight and add the contributions. 0.8 × 0.866 + 0.2 × 0.5 is approximately 0.793. The formula abbreviates these three multiplications and additions. For real colors, repeat the operation for red, green and blue. These are illustrative values, not measured game brightness. Use the same coordinate frame, clamp each dot product to 0–1, then multiply and sum the stored colors. This is the method in Valve’s published 2004 code. Substituting squared weights from another formulation changes the result. We can now follow why small bumps change shading while the stored colors remain unchanged. The final image does not display directional lighting components separately. The game shows the result; the diagram separates the intermediate values producing it. Reading them together makes the storage scheme meaningful. A weight is a mixing proportion. Even with the same ingredients, changing their proportions changes the result. Directional lightmaps give more weight to components aligned with the surface. Here the robot is inspected from different viewpoints. Distinguish surface orientation from camera motion. Materials and lighting also affect the real image. Our diagram isolates surface direction so stored values and the weights used to read them can be considered separately. Changing the normal changes the directional contributions. This adds small-scale orientation response beyond one flat brightness value, without reconstructing geometry or every dynamic occlusion. A single combined value loses directional information. Keeping separate directional components allows a surface to select more of the contribution it faces. This does not independently generate new moving shadows. The game shows completed shading; the diagram separates the directional contributions. Our spatial diagram separates a rock-like surface into actual geometry and normal-map detail. Changing normal arrows affects internal shading while the outer silhouette remains flat. Moving real vertices also changes silhouette and occlusion. The distinction is the information each representation creates. Here we inspect the robot’s arm and torso from different directions. The outline gives clues about geometry, while small variations inside a face give clues about material and orientation. Treating them as the same thing overstates what normal maps can do. Our earlier diagram changed directions without moving the plane’s vertices. Apply the same habit of separating outline from interior detail here. A wall lightmap stays attached to the wall, but a character moves. Lighting can instead be prepared at locations in the room and nearby information retrieved. Such spatial samples are commonly called probes. The historical ambient cube and other engines’ probe systems use different representations. Think of these points as locations storing lighting information, not little light sources. A wall texture stays on a surface; these samples occupy volume, including height. A moving character uses nearby information. Interpolation combines values between samples to avoid abrupt changes. This Unreal example is a different engine from Half-Life 2. As the camera turns into the room, walls and spatial points appear together. Distinguish the lighting image attached to a wall from lighting information sampled in space. The points are not light-emitting bulbs. A later Unreal lighting demonstration displays spatial samples and moves a character between a dark room and a bright floor. A surface-texel grid and samples distributed through space store information in different locations. This is a 2017 engine example of spatial lighting, not the identical implementation of Half-Life 2 ambient cubes. First inspect the character together with the surrounding sample visualization. Locate the prepared values, then follow the character as it changes position. It cannot carry a single wall texel around the room; it needs lighting information appropriate to its location. The room interior and the floor outside have different surroundings and incoming illumination. As the character moves between them, inspect its body brightness together with its position. The displayed samples are spatial clues for this lookup, not necessarily actual light sources. Later, a changed viewpoint reveals the samples and object from another direction. Two points close in the image may be separated in depth. Unlike a surface lightmap, this distribution must be read in height as well. These operations do not measure exact interpolation weights or per-frame cost. Internal values require separate engine evidence. Finally inspect the room from another viewpoint. Consider sample placement together with the places a character can occupy. The existence of samples does not make lighting exact everywhere. Their density, placement and interpolation are further design choices. The key here is that storage is in space rather than on the wall. Higher-quality baking consumes preparation time and storage. Lower runtime cost trades against production work and update cost. One map’s bake time cannot serve as a universal figure for games. Precomputation lets the game read prepared answers. Changing the room or lighting may invalidate them. This editor view inspects a scene; its playback time is not a measurement of baking time. Light remaining after a source is disabled can also reflect different update times. Static indirect light may be stored while direct lighting is updated dynamically. Next, record depth to determine where that changing direct light is blocked. Imagine placing a camera at the light.

scenes.title: 섀도 맵: 같은 점을 광원 좌표에서 검사하기
lines: A shadow map records the first surface depth in each direction instead of color. Comparing a visible surface point against that depth reveals whether another object blocks the light before it arrives. In this example, smaller depth means nearer and larger means farther. A test point behind the stored surface is blocked. Just as rulers need matching origins and units, both depths must be compared using the same light-view convention. Disabling a light differs from disabling shadows. Removing the whole light contribution first darkens the terrain. After restoring it, shadow settings are changed. Distinguish shading caused by surface orientation from shadows cast when another surface blocks light. For a numerical example, stored depth of 0.33 and receiver depth of 0.80 place the receiver behind the first surface. If moving the blocker changes stored depth to 0.90, the receiver at 0.80 lies in front and is unoccluded by this test. Magnifying the light’s depth image reveals its texel grid. Covering a large region with few texels can create stair-stepped shadow edges, even when the original shape is smooth. Stored numbers have limited precision. Two computations of the same surface depth can differ slightly, making it appear to block itself. Bias adds a small adjustment to the comparison to reduce this self-shadowing error. Excessive bias can detach the shadow from the object. A single chosen value is not guaranteed to solve every distance and surface slope. A single shadow-map lookup can give a hard jagged boundary. PCF tests several nearby locations and averages the lit results. It combines comparison outcomes, rather than averaging depths before one comparison. If two of four neighboring tests report visibility, their PCF average is one half. This produces an intermediate visibility value, but does not exactly integrate every path from an area light. Wider filters require more samples and introduce further tradeoffs. A filter’s extent controls the neighborhood combined. PCSS adjusts it using the relationship between blockers and receivers. Variance shadow maps store depth’s first and second moments to approximate visibility. These are different approximations, with limitations such as light leaking in the latter. Variance Shadow Maps and Unreal’s Virtual Shadow Maps share an abbreviation but are different methods. A later episode will distinguish virtual-page shadow management.

scenes.title: 캐스케이드 섀도 맵: 가까운 영역에 더 작은 텍셀
lines: One map covering a broad outdoor scene can make nearby shadows coarse. Cascaded Shadow Maps split the camera’s view by distance and assign shadow maps to those regions. This does not create more lights. It records shadows from one directional light at different spatial densities near and far from the camera. For an illustrative example, 2,048 texels covering 20 meters gives roughly one centimeter per texel. Covering 200 meters with the same count gives roughly ten centimeters. Those numbers are not settings or performance measurements from a game. They illustrate how coverage changes world-space texel size at the same resolution. Choose the shadow map for the point’s camera-distance interval and blend results near transitions. Tiny camera motions can make the projected grid slide and shadows shimmer, so stabilization can snap the projection to the texel grid. In the acquired official Unreal example, the character casts a visible shadow while running on the floor, but not on the stairs. The documentation describes disabled CSM reception on the stairs. That clip demonstrates receiver configuration, rather than visualizing cascade partitions. A separate spatial diagram explains the splits, while the observed engine result illustrates the setting. A 2017 official Unreal demonstration shows the partitions more directly. Enabling Show, Advanced, Shadow Frustums displays differently colored projected boundaries over the scene. Observe how those boundaries change with the shadow distance and distribution controls. The colored boundaries visualize shadow-recording regions, not additional lights. Pulling the camera back reveals the spatial separation between the nearby objects and distant terrain. The same demonstration changes the cascade count through four, zero, one, and three while also adjusting shadow distance. Distinguish disabling cascades from assigning a broad region to one map. Relate the one-versus-multiple edge comparison to our equal-resolution coverage diagram. Several controls change, so we do not attribute every difference to one parameter. Inspect near and far regions together. The total distance and distribution change as well as the number of splits. Connect each visible setting change with the affected region instead of drawing a conclusion from one still image. After the nearby region, inspect distant terrain too. These settings control distant shadow coverage and cascade count. Read the settings together with the region of the view they cover. More cascades require more maps. Managing transitions and stability allocates a budget to shadows. With multiple lights, adding their lighting contributions also has a cost.

scenes.title: 포워드와 디퍼드: 같은 빛을 더하는 다른 순서
lines: That cost is also connected to the order of material and lighting evaluation. Forward rendering evaluates the material and relevant lights while drawing a surface. Once it handles a wall pixel, it completes the lighting calculation there to produce its color. Deferred shading postpones lighting. It first records visible-surface properties such as base color, orientation and depth by image position. This collection is the G-buffer. A later lighting stage reads those records to compute illumination. A buffer stores values for later processing. The G-buffer gathers properties of the visible surface at each image location. Colors in this material view represent specific data rather than decoration; their meaning must be identified. Connect surface information to lighting evaluation and then to the final color. Unwrapping the book assigns image locations to its 3D faces: UV coordinates. Base color describes material color, roughness the spread of reflection, and normals the orientation used in lighting. One surface can have several property images. This is an object-material demonstration, distinct from a screen-space G-buffer. Base color is not the final lit color. Normals encode orientation; roughness controls the spread of a material’s reflection. The Unreal book example inspects and exports material data separately. Object textures and the current frame’s G-buffer use different domains, but the demonstration helps distinguish property types. Follow one pixel on the same wall. Suppose two lighting contributions, already accounting for the material, are 0.25 and 0.35; their sum is 0.6. Forward computes this during surface shading. Deferred records surface data first, then combines lighting in a later stage. The goal is the same; the ordering and intermediate data differ. If a light only reaches the right wall, pixels on the left need not evaluate it. Both approaches can cull irrelevant lights. The four objects and three lights illustrate ordering, not a claim that Forward always evaluates every light or Deferred always wins. S.T.A.L.K.E.R.’s development materials describe a deferred approach for many lights. Its counts and performance figures belong to the documented scene and hardware context. A record is useful to a later operation, but writing and reading it costs work and bandwidth. The G-buffer has that tradeoff. A record of only one frontmost surface cannot by itself describe all the layers needed for transparent glass. Place two glass layers in front of an opaque wall. A buffer storing only the nearest surface does not contain every layer’s material. Compositing them needs additional information or passes. A real engine can therefore combine rendering paths within one frame. A pass is a stage or round of rendering work. An engine can shade opaque objects with Deferred and composite glass in a separate Forward pass. Light pre-pass is another compromise: lighting from depth and normals, followed by material combination. Forward remains in use. Robo Recall is a VR game whose view follows head movement. Its Forward path was chosen with multisampling and required features in mind. We use this demonstration to connect that engineering choice to visible image quality. This is actual VR interaction with objects. Inspect both the response and the image edges. This game illustrates VR’s moving thin edges. Follow the outlines of hands, robots and fragments. Image quality depends on pixel coverage as well as the order of lighting calculations. Next, inspect those edges in the magnified comparison. Anti-aliasing reduces jagged or unstable image edges. Multisampling tests coverage at several positions inside a pixel. If two of four positions are covered, the edge can contribute roughly half the coverage; this is an illustrative example, not a claim about the game’s sample setting. Observe the magnified line. Multiple coverage tests do not necessarily repeat every material and lighting computation that many times. Cost depends on implementation and settings. Forward versus Deferred is therefore a choice involving image quality, features and memory costs, not simply which name is newer. Missing screen-space features in a particular Unreal forward implementation are implementation constraints, not proof that such effects are mathematically impossible in every forward renderer. Changing diagnostic modes reveals information otherwise combined in the final image. This reflection view is not automatically screen-space reflection. Even when effect names resemble one another, their inputs and implementation must be identified. TBDR separates visibility determination from shading; deferred shading separates surface-data storage from lighting. Screen depth retained during rendering can also support effects after lighting. Use that depth to inspect a wall crevice.

scenes.title: 2007: 화면 깊이에서 구석의 가림을 찾는 SSAO
lines: Corners can still look ungrounded after direct-light shadows are drawn because they receive light from fewer surrounding directions than open areas. Screen-space ambient occlusion, or SSAO, estimates this local occlusion from screen depth. Screen-space means operating on information available in the current camera image. SSAO does not trace all lighting through the scene. It examines nearby screen-depth samples to estimate occlusion around a surface. Our diagram places samples around a box corner and compares depths. A small radius emphasizes contact; a larger one reaches farther but can increase undersampling and incorrect associations. Filtering can reduce noise but may blur across boundaries. Sample count, filtering, and depth differences must be considered together. The depth buffer primarily describes visible front surfaces. A thin rod in front of a distant wall does not reveal its thickness through a single depth value. An excessive sample range can associate unrelated surfaces and produce a dark halo around the object. CryEngine 2’s 2007 technical discussion and Unreal documentation describe screen-based approximations and their limitations. Actual comparisons need identified versions and settings. A 2017 Unreal 4.16 demonstration approaches a cube model and changes the AO Power and Bias controls. Watch the gaps between cubes and their floor contacts. Adjusting this contact treatment is different from adding a light source. Several controls and the camera change in this sequence, so we will not attribute every difference to one isolated number. First observe the actual manipulations and contacts; our separate diagram isolates sample range and the limits of depth information. This is not a substitute for direct-light shadows. Darkening corners does not calculate occlusion for a particular lamp or colored indirect light reflected from another wall. Information outside the screen and behind visible surfaces is still missing. The same information boundary becomes important for screen-space reflections in the next episode.

scenes.title: 이번 편의 답과 다음 질문
lines: This episode followed assigned brightness, stored surface lighting, and updated visibility for moving lights. More lights also changed the ordering of material and lighting work. To distinguish methods, ask three questions: what is stored, which changes require recomputation, and which information is missing from the input? The next episode extends the discussion to indirect light, reflections, water, and fog, connecting photon mapping, SSR, Forward+, and clustered lighting to the different problems they address. Reading techniques through their inputs and processing order makes an engine frame easier to understand than names alone. The programming-coaching link in the description is available for hands-on learning.
